en: The *Kamalākara-sarvatathāgata-stotra*.
Then, indeed, in the Lotus Grove, he praised the Blessed Buddhas of the past, future, and present with this hymn to all the Tathāgatas:
"Those Victors who existed in former times, and those who currently abide in the world throughout the ten directions..."
To those Victors I indeed offer prostration, and that assembly of Victors I shall praise. || 1 ||

To the Lord of Munis, peaceful, profoundly tranquil, and pure; whose body is resplendent with the luster of finest gold; who possesses a voice of exquisite sound surpassing all gods and asuras; and whose roar is like the resonance of the voice of Brahmā. (2)
His hair is like a tree frequented by six-legged bees, resembling the dark and beautifully curled kāśa grass;
his teeth are as white as a conch shell or snow, and the luster of his speech shines like gold. (3)
His large, pure, and beautiful eyes were dark blue like a field of blooming blue lotuses;
his lovely tongue shone with the brilliance of gold, and he spoke words as pleasant as the radiance of a lotus.
His navel was like a conch shell or a lotus stalk, a pleasant refuge with its whorls turning to the right;
it was like the subtle moon at the end of the night, the very center of the lotus of Mātra’s beautiful mantra.

I constantly pay homage to that Jina, whose nose is as high as a well-crafted golden balance-beam, whose eyelashes are soft like those of a young deer, and whose tip of the nose is distinguished by its supreme excellence.
Each single hair on his face grows from a single pore, fine, soft, and curling to the right;
his beautiful neck is adorned with a crown resplendent with blue jewels and set with brilliant earrings that appear dark blue.
His body possesses a radiance equal to that of the sun; he is honored throughout all the ten directions of the world;
he has pacified the infinite suffering of the world and has satisfied the world with every form of happiness.
In the hells and among the animal realms, in the worlds of hungry ghosts, gods, asuras, and humans,
may all beings be granted happiness by the Piśācas, and may all states of miserable rebirth be completely pacified.
His complexion is the finest gold, with a luster like refined gold; his body is radiant with the glow of heated gold.
His face is as pure as the gentle moon, and his countenance is as beautiful and stainless as a blooming lotus.
His body was as tender as the tips of young sprouts; he possessed the roar and prowess of a lion in combat;
his arms were long and his hands hung down low; and his tongue was like a *sāla* tree-flame stirred by the wind.
Like the sun blazing with the splendor of the sky and emitting rays, he scorched [all] with his radiance;
the Lord of Munis, with his most pure and excellent body, was infinite and illuminated the entire field.
In infinite thousands of fields, they became a mass of moons, nights, and suns;
and all of them became certain for the sake of the radiant illumination of the Buddhas.
May they behold the Buddha-sun, the lamp illuminating the world, with its thousands of rays of the Buddha-sun, throughout infinite thousands of realms—the sun-like Tathāgata of the world. (14)
Having performed hundreds and thousands of meritorious deeds, his body was adorned with every excellence;
he resembled the lordly elephant of the sun, possessed of conquered arms, and his arms were decorated and protected by stainless [ornaments]. (15)
The Buddhas who have come are like the surface of the earth, equal to the expanse of the fields of rice;
they who are like subtle dust, and they who abide like subtle dust. (16)
With a clear mind, I offer salutations to those Victors with body, speech, and mind;
I remember them with purity through the offering of flowers, the offering of fragrances, and hundreds of pure verses of praise. (17)

Even with a hundred tongues, it would take hundreds of thousands of eons to speak of the qualities of the Buddhas, those perfectly extinguished and sublime Victors; yet that [wisdom] is displayed upon your forehead in its manifold variety.
It is not possible to express even a fraction of the qualities of a single Jina, even with a thousand tongues;
for it is impossible for all the Jinas together to speak at length upon even a single quality.
The entire multitude of all the worlds, including the realm of the gods, and the oceans of existence filled with the waters of all the peaks of becoming—
even if one were able to grasp the measure of those waters, it would not equal even a single fraction of the qualities of the Sugatas.
By this merit accumulated from praising and extolling all the qualities of the Jina’s body and speech with a serene mind, may all sentient beings attain the state of a Victorious One. 21.
Indeed, O King, I make this vow that the entire world shall be awakened by me as a Lord of Men;
and wherever and whenever my birth may occur throughout infinite future eons. (22)
In my dream, I see such a drum and hear such a sound there;
may I obtain such praise of the Jina from Kamalākara, remembering my births and old age there. (23)

The qualities of the Buddha are infinite and incomparable, and though they are difficult to encounter even in a thousand eons, he teaches them— even while engaged in his daily affairs— to those who have heard of them, even in their dreams.

May I liberate sentient beings from the ocean of suffering and fulfill them with the six perfections; may I attain supreme enlightenment and merit, and may the splendor of the royal state be free from all defects. 25.
By the ripening fruit of the gift of the drum and for the sake of praising all the Victors,
may I behold the Lord Śākyamuni face to face and may I receive a prophecy there.
May I obtain, right there, the prophecy of unsurpassed enlightenment for these two boys, my sons, Kanakendra and Kanakaprabhāśvara.

And whatever beings there may be—many and infinite—who are destitute of refuge, fallen into calamity, and without protection, may I become for them everywhere their protector, their ultimate resort, and the giver of refuge in the future. (28)
May I act for the arising of the end of suffering and the source of all happiness throughout future eons, as many as have passed since the prior limit. (29)
By the teaching of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, may my ocean of evil be dried up;
may my ocean of karma be scattered, and may my ocean of afflictions be severed. (30)
May the ocean of my merit be filled; may the ocean of my wisdom be purified. Through the supreme radiance of stainless knowledge, may there be for me the light of desire. (31)
May I possess eyes of radiant merit and become preeminent throughout the entire three worlds;
may I be ever endowed with supreme merit and be a deliverer from the ocean of suffering. (32)
And for an ocean-like eon into the future, may I practice for the sake of all happiness;
through diligent effort, may I reach the limit of the past in such a distinguished field as this within the three worlds. (33)
The *Kamalākara-sarvatathāgata-stotra*, spoken by the illustrious Suvarṇaprabha, is complete.
